title: Ten AI Predictions for 2026: What Leading Analysts Say Legal Teams Should Expect
pub: National Law Review / Jones Walker LLP
author: Andrew R. Lee · Jason M. Loring · Graham H. Ryan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source strongly supports the synthesis: it predicts AI becoming operational infrastructure, identifies in-house departments as faster adopters that may reduce reliance on outside counsel, and stresses strategy, governance, human verification and uncertain ROI. Its claims are largely forecasts and reported survey findings rather than evidence of completed market-wide transformation, matching the synthesis’s cautions.
qs: After two years of experimentation for legal departments, 2026 will be the year AI moves from "interesting tool" to “operational infrastructure,” whether they're ready or not.
The power shift implications are stark: **64% of in-house teams now expect to depend less on outside counsel** because of AI capabilities they're building internally.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified account of substantial task-level automation and evolving lawyer roles without established near-term profession-wide headcount contraction. It also reinforces the need for formal governance, though it does not directly examine the pyramid’s revenue model or apprenticeship pipeline.
qs: Augmentation Wins Over Displacement (For Now)  Despite automation anxieties, Harvard Law School's Center on the Legal Profession found that none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed anticipate reducing the headcount of practicing attorneys, even as some report 100x productivity gains on specific tasks.
But the automation potential remains substantial: McKinsey estimates 22% of a lawyer's job can be automated today, with 44% of legal tasks technically automatable.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: AI is producing substantial task-level and workflow changes without demonstrated near-term wholesale lawyer displacement, while persistent hallucination risk makes human verification and formal governance essential. Its more bullish claims about agentic workflows and operational infrastructure are forecasts, tempered by uncertain ROI and workforce effects.
qs: Augmentation Wins Over Displacement (For Now)  Despite automation anxieties, Harvard Law School's Center on the Legal Profession found that none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed anticipate reducing the headcount of practicing attorneys, even as some report 100x productivity gains on specific tasks.
For legal departments building AI governance frameworks, this means mandatory human review becomes more than just an ethical obligation.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central conclusion that AI is currently augmenting and restructuring legal work rather than broadly displacing lawyers. It cites strong graduate employment and no anticipated practising-attorney headcount cuts among interviewed AmLaw 100 firms, while acknowledging substantial task-automation potential and uncertainty about how quickly roles will evolve. It does not directly substantiate the cluster’s sharper claim about risks to the junior training pipeline.
qs: Augmentation Wins Over Displacement (For Now)  Despite automation anxieties, Harvard Law School's Center on the Legal Profession found that none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed anticipate reducing the headcount of practicing attorneys, even as some report 100x productivity gains on specific tasks.
Roles will evolve; we are all trying to gauge how fast that will happen.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI is becoming operational infrastructure and may strengthen in-house buyer power by reducing dependence on outside counsel. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution that returns remain uneven and scaled adoption requires governance and human verification; its claims are primarily forecasts and reported survey expectations rather than evidence of a completed market-wide shift.
qs: After two years of experimentation for legal departments, 2026 will be the year AI moves from "interesting tool" to “operational infrastructure,” whether they're ready or not.
The power shift implications are stark: **64% of in-house teams now expect to depend less on outside counsel** because of AI capabilities they're building internally.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI adoption requires formal governance grounded in existing professional duties, including competence and verification, rather than informal experimentation. Its broad claim about judicial disclosure requirements is less attentive to the cluster’s emphasis that disclosure remains contested, but this does not alter its overall support.
qs: ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 2024) already established the ethical framework requiring lawyers to have "reasonable understanding" of AI capabilities and limitations.
Informal policies and ad hoc experimentation no longer suffice.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core framing of legal AI as near-term augmentation subject to human verification, professional competence and formal institutional governance. It also reports substantial task-level efficiency gains without treating them as proof of attorney displacement. However, it does not directly examine whether verification costs consume those gains, and its zero-touch contracting forecast is more optimistic than the cluster’s generally supervised framing.
qs: Augmentation Wins Over Displacement (For Now)  Despite automation anxieties, Harvard Law School's Center on the Legal Profession found that none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed anticipate reducing the headcount of practicing attorneys, even as some report 100x productivity gains on specific tasks.
Informal policies and ad hoc experimentation no longer suffice.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly accepts the cluster’s core view that near-term legal AI will augment and redesign work rather than replace lawyers wholesale, while making strategy, workflow integration, governance, human oversight and verification essential. Its stronger forecasts about rapid operationalisation and autonomous agents are less cautious than the cluster’s task-specific, evidence-led framing, but do not displace its overall support for selective, governed deployment.

kp.k: AI shifts from experimentation toward operational infrastructure
kp.d: In this December 31, 2025 client alert, the authors synthesize predictions from Gartner, Forrester, McKinsey and legal technology analysts. Their overarching prediction is that 2026 will move legal departments beyond two years of experimentation, with significant implications for governance, outside counsel relationships and regulatory compliance.
qs: The pilot phase is over.
The implications for AI governance, outside counsel relationships, and regulatory compliance are significant.

kp.k: Agentic systems expand autonomous legal workflows
kp.d: The authors identify autonomous multi-step execution as 2026's most significant technical shift. They report that Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel Legal agentic workflows launch in early 2026 with autonomous document review and Deep Research, while LexisNexis' next-generation Protégé General AI already deploys orchestrator, legal research, web search and customer document agents. Gartner's forecast concerns enterprise applications generally, rather than legal applications alone.
qs: The transition from AI assistants to AI agents that execute multi-step tasks autonomously represents the year's most significant technical shift.
Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by 2026, up from less than 5% today.

kp.k: In-house adoption threatens outside counsel demand
kp.d: The authors assert that corporate legal departments are adopting AI faster than outside counsel. They report ACC/Everlaw survey findings that corporate legal AI adoption rose from 23% to 52% in one year and that 64% of in-house teams expect reduced dependence on outside counsel; the latter is an expectation, not demonstrated work displacement. Everlaw CLO Gloria Lee reports that 60% do not know whether their firms use generative AI on their matters. The authors warn that firms lacking demonstrable capabilities and transparency risk losing work.
qs: The ACC/Everlaw GenAI Survey found corporate legal AI adoption more than doubled in one year, jumping from 23% to 52%.
64% of in-house teams now expect to depend less on outside counsel
60% of in-house teams don't know if their firms use generative AI on their matters
Law firms that can’t demonstrate AI capabilities and transparency on client matters risk losing work to competitors who can.

kp.k: Defined AI strategies correlate with stronger reported outcomes
kp.d: The alert reports Thomson Reuters findings that organizations with defined AI strategies are 2x more likely to experience revenue growth and 3.5x more likely to realize critical AI benefits, while only 22% have achieved strategic clarity. It quotes CEO Steve Hasker's prediction of a divide between adopters and non-adopters in 2026. The document supplies no sample size or methodological detail establishing causation.
qs: Organizations with defined AI strategies are 2x more likely to experience revenue growth and 3.5x more likely to realize critical AI benefits, according to Thomson Reuters.
Yet only 22% of organizations have achieved this strategic clarity.
a new divide among organisations: those that adopt an AI strategy and those that do not.

kp.d: The authors state that August 2026 brings full EU AI Act application to high-risk systems and characterize AI systems used in legal services as falling within that category. They report penalties of €35 million or 7% of global revenue and urge organizations touching the EU market to complete conformity assessments, establish risk management systems and operationalize human oversight. These are the alert's legal characterizations and recommendations.
qs: August 2026 brings full application of the EU AI Act to high-risk systems, and AI systems used in legal services fall squarely within that category.
Penalties reach €35 million or 7% of global revenue.
Organizations must complete conformity assessments, establish risk management systems, and ensure human oversight mechanisms are operational.

kp.k: US state requirements create fragmented compliance obligations
kp.d: The alert states that the Colorado AI Act takes effect in June 2026 with high-risk AI risk management, impact assessment and transparency requirements, and that Illinois's AI in Employment Law requires disclosure when AI influences employment decisions from January 1, 2026. It characterizes a December 2025 Trump Administration executive order as attempting state-law preemption through threatened federal funding withdrawal, while facing constitutional challenges and bipartisan opposition. The authors predict continued compliance fragmentation for national employers pending court resolution.
qs: The Colorado AI Act takes effect in June 2026, requiring risk management policies, impact assessments, and transparency for high-risk AI systems.
Illinois's AI in Employment Law (effective January 1, 2026) mandates disclosure when AI influences employment decisions.
Until courts resolve the federal-state standoff, national employers face a growing patchwork. And the most restrictive requirements set the floor.

kp.k: Near-term augmentation coexists with substantial automation potential
kp.d: The authors report that none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed by Harvard Law School's Center on the Legal Profession anticipated reducing practicing-attorney headcount, despite some reporting 100x productivity gains on specific tasks; the number interviewed is not supplied. They also cite 93% law school graduate employment in 2024, described as a record high. McKinsey's estimates distinguish 22% of a lawyer's job automatable today from 44% of legal tasks technically automatable. The authors favor a near-term augmentation outlook while leaving the pace of role change uncertain.
qs: none of the AmLaw 100 firms interviewed anticipate reducing the headcount of practicing attorneys, even as some report 100x productivity gains on specific tasks.
Law school graduate employment reached 93% in 2024, the highest rate on record.
McKinsey estimates 22% of a lawyer's job can be automated today, with 44% of legal tasks technically automatable.
Roles will evolve; we are all trying to gauge how fast that will happen.

kp.k: Contract automation promises faster review and low-risk autonomy
kp.d: The alert reports that AI integration in contract lifecycle management has already reduced contract cycle times by up to 40%, without identifying the supporting study. Separately, it attributes a potential 50% reduction in contract review time to Gartner and reports analysts' 2026 predictions of zero-touch low-risk contracting, surgical redlining with 95% accuracy and negotiation playbooks matching firm style. These prospective capabilities are distinct from the claimed realized cycle-time reductions.
qs: AI integration in contract lifecycle management has already reduced contract cycle times by up to 40%.
Gartner predicts companies using AI in CLM can cut contract review time by 50%.
For 2026, analysts predict zero-touch contracting for low-risk agreements, surgical redlining achieving 95% accuracy, and AI-generated negotiation playbooks matching firm style.

kp.k: Formal governance replaces ad hoc experimentation
kp.d: Gartner projects that 80% of organizations will formalize AI policies addressing ethical, brand and PII risks by 2026. The authors cite ABA Formal Opinion 512 of July 2024 as requiring reasonable understanding of AI capabilities and limitations, and report that dozens of federal and state judges require AI disclosure and verification through standing orders. They recommend documented, systematic and enforceable governance rather than informal policies.
qs: Gartner projects that by 2026, 80% of organizations will formalize AI policies addressing ethical, brand, and PII risks.
ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 2024) already established the ethical framework requiring lawyers to have "reasonable understanding" of AI capabilities and limitations.
Dozens of federal and state judges have issued standing orders requiring AI disclosure and verification.
Governance must be documented, systematic, and enforceable.

kp.k: Persistent hallucinations make human verification central
kp.d: The alert attributes error rates of 17% for Lexis+ AI and 34% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research to Stanford research, stating that general-purpose models performed worse. Separately, it reports over 700 court cases worldwide involving AI hallucinations, with sanctions ranging from warnings to five-figure monetary penalties; those incidents are distinct from the measured tool error rates. The authors recommend mandatory human review as protection against liability.
qs: Stanford research found error rates of 17% for Lexis+ AI and 34% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research
General-purpose models performed far worse.
Over 700 court cases worldwide now involve AI hallucinations, with sanctions ranging from warnings to five-figure monetary penalties.
For legal departments building AI governance frameworks, this means mandatory human review becomes more than just an ethical obligation. It's now the liability firewall.

kp.k: Weak returns could delay spending and cancel agentic projects
kp.d: The alert contrasts optimistic adoption forecasts with Forrester's prediction that enterprises will defer 25% of planned AI spending into 2027 because of ROI concerns. It reports that only 15% of AI decision-makers saw EBITDA lift in the past 12 months and quotes Forrester research chief Sharyn Leaver's warning about widening gaps between vendor promises and delivered value. Gartner separately predicts cancellation of over 40% of agentic AI projects by the end of 2027 because of costs or unclear business value. These enterprise-wide forecasts underpin the authors' recommendation to prepare for volatility while favoring augmentation.
qs: projecting enterprises will defer 25% of planned AI spend into 2027 due to ROI concerns.
Only 15% of AI decision-makers reported EBITDA lift in the past 12 months.
the gap between inflated vendor promises and value delivered is widening, forcing market correction.
Gartner adds that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027 due to escalating costs or unclear business value.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lee, Loring and Ryan predict that AI will become operational infrastructure in legal departments in 2026, with autonomous agents taking on multi-step workflows.
pts.d: The authors describe a transition from assistants to agents executing tasks autonomously. Their supporting examples are a reported early-2026 launch of CoCounsel Legal agentic workflows for document review and Deep Research, and an already-deployed LexisNexis Protégé configuration comprising four specialized agents. They also report Gartner's enterprise-wide forecast of 40% agent penetration by 2026, compared with less than 5% at the article's reference point; that forecast is not a legal-sector-specific adoption estimate. Legal departments and legal research and document-review practitioners are the principal affected groups.

pts.k: The authors claim faster in-house adoption will shift work and bargaining power away from outside counsel, particularly firms unable to demonstrate AI capabilities and transparency.
pts.d: The authors cite the ACC/Everlaw GenAI Survey for adoption rising from 23% to 52% in one year and for 64% of in-house teams expecting reduced reliance on outside counsel. These are reported adoption levels and expectations, not measured reductions in outside-counsel spending. They also relay a statement from Everlaw's CLO that 60% of in-house teams do not know whether their firms use generative AI on their matters. The prediction concerns corporate legal departments as buyers and competing law firms as providers, with transparency becoming a condition of retaining work.

pts.k: The authors predict that having a defined AI strategy will increasingly distinguish organizational performance in 2026.
pts.d: They report Thomson Reuters findings that organizations with defined AI strategies are twice as likely to experience revenue growth and 3.5 times as likely to realize critical AI benefits, while only 22% have achieved strategic clarity. The article uses these reported associations and an executive statement to support its forecast of a widening divide. It supplies no study methodology or demonstration that strategy caused the reported performance differences. The figures are described as applying to organizations rather than a specified law-firm or legal-department population.

pts.k: The authors claim that EU AI Act requirements will make formal compliance infrastructure necessary for legal-services AI touching the EU market in August 2026.
pts.d: The article characterizes legal-services AI systems as falling within the high-risk category and says full application to high-risk systems arrives in August 2026. It identifies conformity assessments, risk management systems and operational human oversight as required preparations, and reports penalties of up to €35 million or 7% of global revenue. These are the authors' descriptions of regulatory scope, deadlines and exposure; the article does not differentiate particular legal uses or penalty categories.

pts.k: The authors predict a growing US state AI compliance patchwork pending resolution of federal-state legal disputes.
pts.d: They describe Colorado's AI Act as taking effect in June 2026 with risk management, impact assessment and transparency requirements for high-risk systems, and Illinois employment-AI disclosure requirements as effective January 1, 2026. They characterize a December 2025 federal executive order as an attempted preemption facing constitutional challenges and bipartisan opposition. Their conclusion is that national employers must accommodate divergent rules and that the most restrictive requirements establish the practical baseline. This is a claim about employers' compliance environment and the work facing their legal teams, not exclusively about AI used to deliver legal services.

pts.k: The authors favor near-term lawyer augmentation over displacement, while predicting role evolution and leaving its speed uncertain.
pts.d: They cite a Harvard Law School Center on the Legal Profession finding that none of the interviewed AmLaw 100 firms anticipated reducing practicing-attorney headcount, despite some reporting 100-fold productivity gains on particular tasks. That claim concerns the interviewed firms, not necessarily every AmLaw 100 firm. They also report a 93% employment rate for 2024 law graduates and McKinsey estimates that 22% of a lawyer's job can currently be automated and 44% of legal tasks are technically automatable. The article presents these as distinct measures; technical automation potential is not itself an observed job-loss figure.

pts.k: The authors predict faster and increasingly autonomous contracting, including zero-touch handling of low-risk agreements in 2026.
pts.d: The article reports that AI integration in contract lifecycle management has already shortened contract cycles by up to 40%, without identifying the underlying study in the supplied text. It relays Gartner's prediction of a possible 50% reduction in review time for companies using AI in CLM. It attributes 2026 predictions of zero-touch low-risk contracting, 95%-accurate surgical redlining and firm-style negotiation playbooks to analysts without specifying which analysts or how accuracy is measured. These claims affect corporate contracting teams, legal reviewers and organizations competing on contracting efficiency. Zero-touch contracting is substitution for a bounded workflow, unlike the article's broader augmentation framing.

pts.k: The authors argue that documented AI governance is becoming required infrastructure rather than an optional best practice.
pts.d: They relay Gartner's projection that 80% of organizations will formalize AI policies by 2026 to address ethical, brand and personally identifiable information risks. For lawyers specifically, they cite ABA Formal Opinion 512 from July 2024 and standing orders issued by dozens of federal and state judges requiring AI disclosure and verification. These authorities support their prescription for systematic, enforceable governance; the Gartner adoption projection is separate from their claim about legal and ethical obligations. Affected groups include organizational leadership, legal departments and lawyers subject to applicable professional duties and court orders.

pts.k: The authors claim persistent hallucination risks make mandatory human review central to legal departments' liability management.
pts.d: They report Stanford research error rates of 17% for Lexis+ AI and 34% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, and state that general-purpose models performed substantially worse. Separately, they report more than 700 court cases worldwide involving AI hallucinations, with sanctions from warnings to five-figure monetary penalties. The supplied text does not identify the court-case tracker, measurement dates or study methods. The measured tool error rates and the count of court incidents are different forms of evidence. Their recommendation concerns human verification of output before reliance, not model benchmarking.

pts.k: The authors anticipate an AI investment correction driven by weak realized returns, rising costs and uncertain business value.
pts.d: They report Forrester's prediction that enterprises will defer 25% of planned AI spending into 2027 because of ROI concerns, alongside a finding that only 15% of AI decision-makers reported EBITDA improvement in the preceding 12 months. They also relay Gartner's forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs or unclear value. These are enterprise-wide findings and forecasts used to qualify the article's legal-sector outlook, not legal-specific spending or cancellation estimates. Legal teams and organizations procuring AI are urged to prepare for volatility despite the near-term augmentation thesis.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source is an authorial synthesis of third-party surveys, research, forecasts, product announcements and regulatory authorities rather than an original empirical study.
pts.d: Lee, Loring and Ryan support their predictions with ACC/Everlaw adoption and expectation data; Thomson Reuters strategy-performance figures; Harvard interview findings; employment statistics; McKinsey automation estimates; Stanford legal-tool error measurements; court incidents; and legislation, ethics guidance and judicial orders. Gartner and Forrester forecasts supply much of the forward-looking quantitative evidence. Product examples support claims about agentic functionality. Some figures, including the 40% contract-cycle reduction, 95% redlining accuracy prediction and worldwide hallucination-case count, lack a specified underlying source or methodology in the supplied text. The authors' conclusions about power shifts, competitive disadvantage and governance are their synthesis of this material, rather than independently measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The main forecast horizon is 2026, with historical and current indicators used as support and investment risks extending through 2027.
pts.d: The alert is dated December 31, 2025. Its retrospective evidence includes 2024 graduate employment, July 2024 ethics guidance, one-year adoption growth and EBITDA reports covering the preceding 12 months. Specific future milestones include early-2026 CoCounsel workflows, January 2026 Illinois requirements, June 2026 Colorado requirements and August 2026 EU requirements, as described by the authors. Spending deferrals extend into 2027 and agentic project cancellations through the end of 2027. Important qualifications are augmentation 'for now'; productivity gains limited to specific tasks; zero-touch contracting limited to low-risk agreements; compliance exposure conditioned on market or jurisdictional reach; and investment retrenchment conditioned on costs and business value. The article does not give exact data-collection dates for most supporting statistics.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, outside law firms, practicing lawyers, contracting teams and employers with multijurisdictional obligations.
pts.d: In-house teams are portrayed as gaining internal capability and leverage over outside providers while taking on governance and verification responsibilities. Law firms face potential work loss if they lack demonstrable capabilities or transparency; interviewed large firms nonetheless anticipate maintaining practicing-attorney headcount. Lawyers' research, document-review and contracting tasks may become faster or more automated. Corporate contracting teams may use autonomous processing for low-risk agreements. EU-facing organizations and national US employers face compliance preparation and overlapping requirements. Enterprise AI buyers face uncertain returns and possible spending deferrals or project cancellations. The article does not offer a separate claim about access to justice, unmet individual legal needs, ALSP market shares or changes to law-firm staffing shapes.
